title: The Brothers Bow Before Joseph
summary: The famine drives Jacob to send ten of his sons to Egypt for grain, though he keeps Benjamin at home. Joseph recognizes his brothers when they bow before him, but they do not recognize him; he accuses them of spying, holds them in custody for three days, and keeps Simeon until they bring their youngest brother. The silver they find returned in their sacks fills them with dread, and Jacob refuses to let Benjamin go.
story: More than twenty years have passed since the brothers sold Joseph (Genesis 37). He was seventeen then; he was thirty when Pharaoh raised him up, and the seven years of plenty have come and gone. Now the dreams that began the story start to come true in plain sight: the brothers arrive and bow down with their faces to the ground, and the narrator notes that “Joseph remembered his dreams about them.” But fulfillment is not the same as reconciliation. The family God chose to carry his promise to Abraham is broken by envy, a crime, and a long lie told to their father. The question that drives the next three chapters is whether these men have changed, and in particular whether they will abandon Rachel's other son, Benjamin, as they once abandoned Joseph. This chapter opens that test and ends with Simeon in an Egyptian prison and Jacob refusing to risk his youngest.
historical:
Egypt was the breadbasket of the eastern Mediterranean world. Canaan depended on rainfall, which could fail for years at a time, while Egypt's harvests depended on the Nile, which drew on rains far to the south. People of Canaan going down to Egypt in famine is a pattern Genesis has already shown (Abraham in Genesis 12:10), and Egyptian records confirm that herders from the east sought food and pasture in the Delta in hard times.

Joseph's accusation that the brothers are spies would have sounded plausible in Egypt. The Nile Delta's eastern edge was the country's most exposed frontier, the route by which invaders from Canaan and beyond entered. The Egyptian Story of Sinuhe, a Middle Kingdom tale, mentions the Walls of the Ruler, a line of border defenses built to keep out the peoples of the northeast. A group of ten men from Canaan asking questions at the royal granaries could easily be treated as a scouting party.
cultural:
Joseph swears “as surely as Pharaoh lives”, the oath of an Egyptian official, which helps hide his identity. He speaks through an interpreter, which is why the brothers talk freely in front of him. Holding one man hostage to guarantee that others would return was a common way to secure an agreement. The silver in the sacks was not coinage (coins were not invented until centuries later, in the seventh century BC in Asia Minor); it was weighed metal carried in tied bundles, which is why each man finds his bundle intact.

The brothers' speech reflects a world in which shed blood cried out for an answer. Reuben says, “Now we must account for his blood!”, the language of blood guilt that runs from Abel (4:10) through God's word to Noah (9:5-6). As the eldest, Reuben bore responsibility for his younger brothers, but his offer that Jacob may kill his two sons if he fails to bring Benjamin back is rash and useless; no grandfather would accept it. Sheol, in Jacob's final words, is the Old Testament's name for the realm of the dead, the grave seen as a place all go down to.
literary: The chapter is built to echo Genesis 37. Then the brothers stripped Joseph and threw him into a pit; now they are held in custody. Then they heard his cries and ignored them; now we learn for the first time that he pleaded with them (v. 21), a detail the earlier chapter left out. Then they came home with silver from selling him; now silver appears in their sacks and terrifies them. The key word is recognize. Joseph “recognized them”, but they “did not recognize him” (v. 8), and he made himself a stranger to them using a related Hebrew form. The same verb was used when the brothers told Jacob to recognize Joseph's bloodied robe (37:32). Dramatic irony runs throughout, since the reader knows what the brothers do not. The chapter also contains the brothers' first mention of God in the Joseph story: “What is this that God has done to us?” (v. 28). Their report to Jacob (vv. 29-34) softens what happened, leaving out the three days in custody and Simeon being bound before their eyes.

outline.t: Jacob sends ten sons to Egypt for grain
Joseph recognizes his brothers and accuses them
Simeon is held and the brothers confess their guilt
The report to Jacob and his refusal to send Benjamin

doctrines.note: The brothers' crime has not faded in twenty years. Put under pressure, they immediately connect their distress with what they did to Joseph. Sin in Genesis is not only an act in the past but a weight that remains, shaping a family's fear and silence until it is faced.

“Surely we are being punished because of our brother” (v. 21) is the first honest word the brothers speak about Joseph. It is not yet full repentance, which the story will show in Judah's willingness to suffer for Benjamin (44:33), but it is the beginning: guilt named aloud, together, without excuse.

The dreams of Genesis 37 are fulfilled by the very men who tried to stop them. The brothers see God's hand only as threat (v. 28), but the reader knows that God is working through the famine and through Joseph to save them. Providence often looks like judgment to those who have not yet faced their guilt.

words.note: Nakar, to recognize or regard. Joseph recognized his brothers; they did not recognize him (vv. 7-8). A related form of the same root means to make oneself a stranger, which is what Joseph does. The verb links the Joseph story together: the brothers asked Jacob to recognize the robe (37:32), and Tamar asked Judah to recognize his seal and staff (38:25). Each time, recognition brings hidden guilt into the open.

Ashem, guilty. The brothers' words in verse 21 begin, in Hebrew, with the admission that they are truly guilty concerning their brother. The word belongs to the same family later used in Leviticus for the guilt offering, which dealt with wrongs that needed to be made right. Here it marks the moment the brothers stop defending themselves.

Bachan, to test or examine, often used of testing metal to see what it truly is. Joseph says the brothers' words will be tested (vv. 15-16). Elsewhere the Old Testament uses the verb of God testing hearts (Psalm 139:23; Jeremiah 17:10). Joseph's test is designed to reveal whether the brothers have changed.

christ: This chapter gives no prediction of Christ, but it shows the shape of the reconciliation the gospel offers. Joseph holds power over the men who wronged him, and he uses it not for revenge but to bring their buried guilt into the light, because there can be no real reunion while the truth stays hidden. His harsh words are matched by private tears (v. 24). Christian readers have seen in Joseph, unrecognized by the brothers who rejected him, a likeness to the one who came to his own and was not received (John 1:11), and to the risen Jesus, whom his disciples did not at first recognize (Luke 24:16). The likeness is thematic rather than predictive, and its point is the same in both stories: the one who was wronged is the one who comes, at cost to himself, to restore those who wronged him.

hard.q: Why does Joseph treat his brothers so harshly? Is he taking revenge?
hard.a:
The text never states Joseph's motives directly. It says he remembered his dreams (v. 9), spoke harshly (v. 7), and wept in private (v. 24), and it leaves the reader to weigh these together. The most common reading is that Joseph is testing his brothers. He needs to know whether they have changed before he can trust them, and the test he designs recreates the situation of Genesis 37: will they leave a brother behind in bondage to save themselves, and will they sacrifice Rachel's other son? Their response in chapter 44 shows that the test served reconciliation.

Other readers think the narrator is also showing a wounded man working through his own pain, with genuine anger mixed into the testing, which would explain why he imprisons all of them at first (v. 17) and then changes his plan (vv. 18-20). Some suggest that Joseph is trying to bring about his dreams, in which all eleven brothers bow, so that Benjamin must come. These readings are not exclusive. Genesis presents Joseph as a real man, not a flawless saint, and the tears in verse 24 suggest that whatever else he felt, he still loved them.

questions: The brothers' guilt surfaced more than twenty years after they sold Joseph. What does this chapter suggest about what happens to wrongs that are buried rather than confessed?
Joseph wept in private while speaking harshly in public. When is hard testing a form of love, and when does it become something else?
Jacob says, “Everything is going against me!” at the very moment God is working to save his family. How do you read your own circumstances when they seem to say the same thing?
